title: Prompt Engineering for Repeatable Technical Work
content:
A repeatable technical prompt is a small work specification. It tells an AI system what task to perform, what material it may use, what output is acceptable, and how uncertainty should appear. A polished instruction cannot make a model infallible. It can make failures easier to detect and comparisons between versions more meaningful. For technical work, that is more useful than chasing a single clever phrase.

Specify the job and its boundaries

Begin with a concrete verb and object: classify a support ticket, summarize a change log, or propose tests for a function. State the audience and the decision the output supports. Provide the necessary input in a clearly delimited section and say whether the model may use outside knowledge. If the answer must be grounded only in supplied documentation, require citations to those documents and an explicit “insufficient information” path. Do not ask for certainty when the evidence is missing.

Write constraints that can be checked. A useful instruction might require three fields named issue, evidence, and next_step; a JSON schema may be appropriate if software consumes the result. For human readers, a short sectioned answer may be better. Avoid piling up contradictory demands such as “be exhaustive” and “use one sentence” without stating priority. Include the action to take when a required field cannot be supported.

OpenAI's prompt-engineering guide discusses instructions, context, examples, and output format as parts of a prompt. The guide gives techniques, not a guarantee that any wording will prevent an incorrect technical answer.

Use examples to define edge cases

One ordinary example can demonstrate format, but it may also teach a narrow pattern that does not generalize. Add examples that distinguish similar cases: a supported claim versus an unsupported one, a missing input versus a negative result, and a valid command versus a destructive command that needs review. Do not include secrets or real customer records in examples without authorization. Make examples realistic enough to test the actual task, yet simple enough that a reviewer can explain why each expected answer is correct.

Separate durable instructions from variable task data. A stable instruction block should describe the role, constraints, and output contract. Variable content should contain the current ticket, document, or code fragment. This separation supports versioning and makes it easier to identify whether a changed answer came from the instructions or the input. Record model and configuration alongside prompt version when comparing outputs; otherwise a prompt comparison may attribute a behavior change to the wrong cause.

Test behavior rather than elegance

Create a small evaluation set before calling a prompt “ready.” Include straightforward tasks, ambiguous requests, missing context, and cases where the correct response is to ask for more information. Write what good output must contain and what unacceptable output looks like. Run the same cases after every substantive prompt change. Inspect individual failures rather than relying only on a summary score. A fluent answer that cites a source incorrectly is a failure even when the prose looks professional.

OpenAI's evals documentation describes testing model behavior against use-case examples. A versioned evaluation set supports comparison, while human review remains important for nuanced technical correctness.

Distinguish a deterministic format check from a quality judgment. A JSON parser can confirm syntactic validity; it cannot establish that a recommended database migration is safe. For high-impact tasks, pair automated validation with domain review and a deployment gate. Record the model's uncertainty and your own review outcome. If the system can run tools, limit their permissions and inspect proposed actions before irreversible execution.

A hypothetical code-review prompt

Suppose a hypothetical team asks a model to review a pull request. The first prompt says only “find bugs,” producing broad guesses. A revised specification supplies the changed files, relevant test output, and the repository's supported runtime. It asks for findings with file location, triggering condition, observed evidence, and severity; it allows “no substantiated finding.” An evaluation case includes a deliberate regression, a harmless refactor, and a missing dependency detail that should trigger uncertainty.

This hypothetical example does not claim that the revised prompt catches every bug. It makes feedback more inspectable. Reviewers still run tests and examine code. If the model invents a failure mode, the team adds that case to the evaluation set and updates the prompt or workflow only after understanding the cause. They do not silently reward an answer for listing more findings.

Keep a practical prompt checklist

Before reuse, confirm the intended task and audience; input provenance; allowed sources; expected output format; treatment of missing evidence; constraints on tool use; examples of acceptable refusal or uncertainty; evaluation cases; and a named reviewer for high-impact outcomes. Check that the prompt does not ask the model to claim personal testing or access it did not have. When a task changes, revisit the specification rather than appending another instruction at the end.

Treat prompt engineering as maintenance. Inputs, models, tools, and organizational rules change, so version the prompt with its tests and review failures over time. A stable template can reduce avoidable ambiguity, but it cannot replace evidence, access controls, or human judgment. The strongest technical workflow makes it easy to see both what the model was asked to do and what still needs independent verification.
